items.followUp: Define % mass/volume and write its formula.

rubric.why: The definition must identify both the solute volume and the total solution volume.
rubric.description: Defines volume/volume percentage as the volume of solute in 100 volumes of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or equivalent formula.

rubric.why: The formula expresses the definition quantitatively.
rubric.description: Gives the formula for % v/v.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio multiplied by 100.

modelAnswer: % volume/volume is the volume of solute present in 100 volumes of solution.
% v/v = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100.

items.followUp: What is the Tyndall effect, and how can it help distinguish a colloid from a true solution?

rubric.why: A colloid scatters light, making the path of a beam visible.
rubric.description: Describes shining a beam of light through the sample and observing its path.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct test.

rubric.why: The visible beam path is the observation that identifies a colloid.
rubric.description: States that a visible light path due to scattering (the Tyndall effect) indicates a colloid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct observation and conclusion.

modelAnswer: Pass a beam of light through the given solution in a dark room.
If the path of the beam becomes visible due to scattering of light (the Tyndall effect), the sample is a colloidal solution.

rubric.why: Gold is commonly used to make jewellery and ornaments.
rubric.description: Gives one suitable application of gold in jewellery or ornaments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct application.

rubric.why: Gold is also used in dental work and electrical/electronic components.
rubric.description: Gives another suitable application of gold.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second correct application.

modelAnswer: Gold is used to make jewellery and ornaments.
Gold is used in dentistry and in electrical/electronic components.

items.followUp: Name one naturally occurring compound of sodium and one of calcium.

rubric.why: Both groups contain reactive metals, so they occur naturally in combined form rather than as free elements.
rubric.description: States that alkali metals and alkaline earth metals occur in nature as compounds, not free elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct general occurrence.

rubric.why: Examples should include a compound of an alkali metal and a compound of an alkaline earth metal.
rubric.description: Gives suitable occurrence examples for both groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example from each group.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals are highly reactive, so they occur in nature in the combined state, not as free elements.
Alkali metals occur in compounds such as sodium chloride and potassium chloride; alkaline earth metals occur in compounds such as calcium carbonate and magnesium carbonate.

items.followUp: How does the electropositive character of elements change down a group and across a period?

rubric.why: Electropositive character increases as one moves down a group.
rubric.description: Gives the trend down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

rubric.why: Electropositive character decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.description: Gives the trend across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

modelAnswer: In a group, electropositive character increases from top to bottom.
Across a period, electropositive character decreases from left to right.

items.followUp: Write five properties of canal rays.

rubric.why: Straight-line travel is a characteristic property of cathode rays.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles and are deflected toward a positive plate.
rubric.description: States their negative charge and response to an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Their properties do not depend on the gas in the tube or the electrode material.
rubric.description: States that cathode-ray properties are independent of the gas and electrodes used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays produce fluorescence when they strike certain materials.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays cause fluorescence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays have energy and can produce mechanical effects or penetrate thin materials.
rubric.description: States another correct property, such as rotating a paddle wheel or penetrating thin metal foil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one additional correct property.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
They are negatively charged and are deflected toward the positive plate in an electric field.
Their properties are independent of the nature of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
They possess kinetic energy; for example, they can rotate a light paddle wheel.

items.followUp: Write four properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points because the forces between their molecules are weak.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct general property.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally lack mobile ions or electrons to carry charge.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct general property.

rubric.why: Most covalent compounds are insoluble in water.
rubric.description: States their usual solubility in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct general property.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds are generally soluble in organic solvents; many are also volatile or soft.
rubric.description: States solubility in organic solvents and one further suitable property, such as volatility or softness.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for solubility in organic solvents and 1 mark for another correct property.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points because the forces between their molecules are weak.
They generally do not conduct electricity because they have no mobile ions or electrons.
Most are insoluble in water.
They are generally soluble in organic solvents.
Many covalent compounds are volatile or soft.

items.followUp: Define allotropy and explain why an element may show it, giving one example of a transition temperature.

rubric.why: Allotropy concerns different forms of the same element in the same physical state.
rubric.description: Defines allotropy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential definition.

rubric.why: Different atomic or molecular arrangements and crystal structures can produce distinct forms of an element.
rubric.description: Gives a structural reason for allotropy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct reason.

rubric.why: Allotropic forms may also differ in the number or grouping of atoms in their molecules.
rubric.description: Gives a further valid reason for allotropy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an additional correct reason.

accept: changes from one allotropic form to another
rubric.why: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another; sulphur provides a standard example.
rubric.description: Defines transition temperature, with the transition of rhombic sulphur to monoclinic sulphur at about 96°C as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition or a correct example.

modelAnswer: Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
These forms may differ because their atoms are arranged differently or form different molecular structures and crystal arrangements.
The temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another is called the transition temperature.
For example, rhombic sulphur changes into monoclinic sulphur at about 96°C.
